claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 exists as a disordered BCC phase at high temperature.
The high-temperature disordered BCC phase is thermodynamically metastable.
Al induces a thermodynamic driving force for ordering and eventual phase transformation in this alloy.
Phase stability is governed by competition between the thermodynamic driving force for ordering and kinetic hindrance of atomic diffusion during cooling.
Sufficient diffusion time during cooling permits formation of B2 or another ordered intermetallic arrangement.
Formation of an ordered arrangement lowers the alloy's free energy relative to the disordered BCC state.
Rapid cooling kinetically suppresses ordering and phase transformation.
Slow cooling allows Al and possibly other elements to redistribute by diffusion.
Slow cooling produces an ordered phase or mixed-phase equilibrium favored thermodynamically at lower temperatures.
Rapid quenching preserves the initial BCC state even though that state is thermodynamically unstable at lower temperatures.
Slow-cooled samples will contain significantly more ordered/intermetallic phase or secondary precipitates than quenched samples.
Quenched samples will largely retain the disordered BCC phase.
Ordering or secondary-phase formation can be distinguished using XRD and electron microscopy.
The proposed transformation occurs below the high-temperature homogenization regime but above temperatures at which diffusion is effectively frozen.
The observed phase fractions are sensitive to cooling rate.
Two sample sets should be prepared from the same homogenized batch and subjected respectively to slow cooling and rapid quenching.
Failure of slow cooling to produce a statistically significant increase in ordered/intermetallic phase fraction relative to quenching would falsify the proposed mechanism.
